opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the really interesting open questions, and it's something I think about a lot from the architecture side. If you look at a robot, it's dealing with information at wildly different rates. At the lowest level you have motor control and proprioception, things happening at hundreds of hertz or even a kilohertz, where you need very fast, very reactive responses. Then you have perception, vision coming in at maybe tens of frames per second. And then at the top you have planning and reasoning: "I'm making breakfast, I need to get the eggs out of the fridge first." That's operating on the scale of seconds, minutes, sometimes longer.

I don't think a single monolithic transformer processing every token at the same rate is the right answer there. Attention is quadratic, and if you try to put every high-frequency sensor reading into one giant context, it just gets too expensive and too slow for real-time control. So what I find compelling is some kind of hierarchical design. You might have a fast, small model, maybe something recurrent or state-space-like, because those have constant memory and constant time per step, handling the low-level control loop. Then a slower, larger model that does the higher-level reasoning and only updates every so often, passing down goals or latent commands to the fast layer.

That's actually part of why I've been excited about state space models and these hybrid architectures. A recurrent state is a natural fit for streaming data: you compress the history into a fixed-size state and keep going, which is exactly what you want for a control loop that never stops. But pure recurrent models can struggle with precise recall over long horizons, so mixing in some attention layers, or having a slower attention-based planner on top, gives you a nice balance.

There's also a systems angle people underestimate. Even if you have the right architecture on paper, you need inference to be fast and predictable on the hardware actually on the robot. Latency matters a lot more than throughput there. So co-designing the model with the hardware, thinking about memory bandwidth, how big the state is, how often each component runs, is going to be really important.

Honestly, I don't think we've figured it out yet. A lot of current robotics foundation models are adapted from language and vision models and then bolted onto an action head. I suspect over the next few years we'll see architectures designed natively for multi-timescale problems, and that's going to be a big unlock.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a small, fast model for low-level control and a slower, larger model for higher-level planning and reasoning, communicating the requested difference in computation across time scales.

r002.rationale: It describes inputs such as proprioception and vision and proposes a hierarchy of control and planning models, but does not clearly envision composing models from different modalities.

r003.rationale: The response calls the architecture an open question, but does not identify how to integrate component models as a central unresolved question; it instead sketches a hierarchical design.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions in robotics right now, and it maps surprisingly well onto things we've been thinking about on the sequence modeling side.

So if you look at what a robot actually has to do, there's this huge spread of time scales. At the very bottom you've got low-level control, torque commands, balance, things running at hundreds of hertz, maybe a kilohertz. Then there's something like manipulation and motion planning, which is more like tens of hertz. And then at the top you have task planning and reasoning, "go to the kitchen, find the cup, bring it back," which happens on the scale of seconds or minutes, and where you can afford to be slow and deliberate.

The naive thing is to say, okay, one big model, run it at the fastest rate, let it figure everything out. And that just doesn't work, for a couple of reasons. One is compute. You can't run a large vision-language model at a kilohertz on an embedded GPU, and you probably shouldn't want to. The other is that the statistics of these problems are genuinely different. Low-level control is smooth, reactive, mostly local in time. High-level planning is discrete, sparse, needs long context and world knowledge. Forcing one architecture to be good at both is fighting against the structure of the problem.

So I think the architecture should be explicitly hierarchical, and I'd argue the levels should be different kinds of models, not just the same model at different sizes. At the fast layer, you want something with constant memory and constant time per step. This is where recurrent or state-space style models are a really natural fit. You have a compressed state of the recent past, you update it every tick, you emit an action, and you never touch anything that grows with history. That's exactly the regime where you want to be hardware-efficient and predictable in latency. You basically want it to look like a controller, and these models can be trained end-to-end to be that controller.

At the slow layer, attention-style models make a lot of sense, because the thing you care about is recalling specific things: where did I see the cup, what did the person ask for, what did I try before that failed. That's a retrieval problem, and attention is good at retrieval. You're running it infrequently enough that the cost is fine.

And then the interesting design question is the interface between layers. I think the right abstraction is that the slow model writes a goal or a latent conditioning signal that persists for some horizon, and the fast model consumes it as part of its state. The fast model doesn't need to re-derive the plan every millisecond, it just needs to track it. And information has to flow back up too, the slow model needs some summary of what happened at the fast level, but that summary can be very compressed. You don't want to feed a kilohertz of proprioception into your planner.

The other thing I'd point out is that there's a nice connection to how we think about memory in sequence models. Compressed recurrent state versus explicit KV cache is kind of the same dichotomy as fast reflexive control versus slow deliberate recall. Hybrid architectures, where you mix a few attention layers into a mostly state-space backbone, are sort of the single-model version of this hierarchy. So I'm actually fairly optimistic that some of the lessons from building efficient language models transfer pretty directly. The constraints are just much more brutal in robotics: you have a hard real-time budget, limited power, and the cost of being wrong is physical.

The last thing I'd say is, I think you should let the data decide where the boundaries go, at least partly. The human-designed hierarchy, 1 kHz, 10 Hz, 0.1 Hz, is a reasonable prior, but I'd want the training setup to allow the slow module to run more often when things are uncertain and less often when things are routine. Adaptive compute across time scales, basically. We're not fully there yet, but that's the direction I find most compelling.

r001.rationale: The response assigns fast, low-level control a constant-time, hardware-efficient controller and reserves the more costly attention model for infrequent, deliberate high-level planning.

r002.rationale: It proposes combining different kinds of models, such as recurrent or state-space models and attention models, but does not describe combining models from different modalities.

r003.rationale: It calls the interface between layers an interesting design question and explains how goals and compressed feedback could flow between the slow and fast models.

astra-6.text:
I think you probably want a hierarchy. Some things need to happen very quickly—if the robot starts losing its balance, you can't wait for a big model to reason about what to do. You need a fast control loop that responds to the sensors. Then other things, like deciding how to pick up an object or planning a sequence of actions, can operate at a slower rate.

So you might have a larger model doing the planning and a smaller model executing those plans, with feedback going both ways. The interesting question is how they communicate. What does the planner need to tell the controller, and when does the controller need to say, “Hey, something changed; we need a new plan”? I’d think about the architecture in terms of those different time scales, rather than assuming one model should make every decision at the same frequency.

r001.rationale: It proposes a fast, smaller control model and a larger, slower planning model, communicating the allocation of less model capacity to execution than planning.

r002.rationale: It describes planning and control models but does not say the architecture combines models from different modalities.

r003.rationale: It explicitly calls how the planner and controller communicate an interesting question and asks what each should tell the other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you probably want a hierarchy, because the different parts of the problem have very different latency requirements. If the robot is balancing or reacting to contact, that control loop needs to run very quickly. You don’t want it waiting for a large model to finish reasoning about what to do next.

Then, at a slower time scale, you can have a model that figures out the next action or skill, and above that, something that plans over a longer horizon—what am I trying to accomplish, and how should I break that down?

The interesting question is how those pieces communicate. The fast controller needs enough autonomy to respond to the environment, while the slower planner needs feedback when its assumptions stop being true. So I’d think of it as multiple systems running asynchronously, with different compute budgets and different update rates, rather than one model making every decision.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a fast control loop with slower planning, but does not specify allocating less computation to joint control than to route planning.

r002.rationale: It describes multiple systems at different time scales, but does not identify models from different modalities.

r003.rationale: It calls how the pieces communicate “the interesting question” and describes feedback between the fast controller and slower planner.
